name: The north door yews of St Edward's, Stow-on-the-Wold

location.address: St Edward's Church, Church Street, Stow-on-the-Wold, Gloucestershire GL54 1BB

access: Open churchyard (Ancient Yew Group lists access as public; church parochial church council ground). Free, no opening hours. The yews stand at the church's north door; the church is in the centre of the town, a few minutes from the Square.
transport: In the centre of Stow-on-the-Wold, 2 minutes' walk from the Square. Bus links from Cheltenham and Moreton-in-Marsh (mainline station about 6 km away).
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the door they frame, two yew trunks pressed against either side of the arched north door of St Edward's. They stand on the church's north side, a few minutes from the Square.
verify_notes: AYG (Tim Hills, visited 14 Jan 2006): two male yews grow close to and either side of the north door; they feature in Thomas Pakenham's Meetings with Remarkable Trees; girths at 4 ft were 6 ft 5 in and 6 ft 7 in (196 and 201 cm; girth_cm records the larger). Earliest mention 1897 (Birmingham and Warwickshire Archaeological Society): 'the two ancient yew trees which seem to embrace the entrance are curious'. Stow Civic Society: the north porch was built about 300 years ago and young yew saplings were planted to enhance the entrance; the trees now form part of the architraves of the door. CONFLICT: 1897 calls them ancient, the civic society gives about 300 years; age kept at about 300, from the civic society, broad. Famous as the 'Tolkien door' (rumoured inspiration for the Doors of Durin): Stow Civic Society says 'rumoured'; Gloucester diocese and others say unconfirmed, so state it only as a rumour. Diocese of Gloucester 2022 piece names them as the 'ancient trees' dedicated to the Queen for the Platinum Jubilee (page text not fully read: only its title, flag). Alive: AYG tree page carries photos by Jane Bridgman dated 2025. Position: AYG six-figure grid SP191258 (100 m), converted; church pin approximate. Girth is at 4 ft (122 cm) as recorded; both trunks fused with the door arch. Writing pass 2026-11-04: lead photo Geograph 5256872 (Colin Smith, 2015) approved; Geograph 8417263 (Brian Deegan, 2026-09-19) shows both yews standing but is underexposed.
story:
Nobody has proved that Tolkien ever stood at this door, and the door hardly needs him. Two yews grow tight against the north porch of St Edward's, one on each side, and over the centuries their trunks have become part of the doorframe. The stone arch sits between them like something they are holding up. Locals call it the Tolkien door, and Stow Civic Society says it is rumoured to have inspired the Doors of Durin in The Lord of the Rings. Rumoured is the honest word, and the Diocese of Gloucester calls the link unconfirmed.

How old the pair are is a real disagreement. The civic society says the porch was built about 300 years ago and young yews were planted to dress the entrance. Yet in 1897 a visiting archaeological society already called them ancient, two trees which seem to embrace the entrance. We follow the civic society and keep the band broad, roughly 250 to 350 years.

They are not huge. When the Ancient Yew Group measured them in 2006, the two male trunks were 196 and 201 centimetres round at four feet, slim by churchyard standards. Thomas Pakenham put them in Meetings with Remarkable Trees anyway, and you can see why. Plenty of churchyard yews stand beside a door. These two have grown into the frame.
